blocks.value: The `while` loop repeats a block of statements while a given condition evaluates to true. It evaluates the condition **before** executing the loop body.

The expression is the loop condition, enclosed in parentheses; it may be a relational or logical expression returning `true` or `false`. The statements in braces are the **loop body**, which may be a simple or compound statement.

The expression provides an **entry condition**. If it evaluates to `true`, the body executes and the expression is re-evaluated. The body continues to execute until the expression evaluates to `false`.
`num` is the **loop control variable**: a variable whose value determines whether loop execution continues. Within the body, `num++` updates it until the condition evaluates to `false`.
A loop that continues to execute endlessly is an **infinite loop**. To avoid one, ensure the loop body contains statements that guarantee the condition will eventually become false.
Three things make a `while` loop terminate, and all three must be present:

items: The control variable is **initialised** before the loop.
The body **changes** it, in the direction that makes the condition false.

blocks.value: Drop any one and the loop never ends. If a program hangs, press `Ctrl+C` and check those three.
